options.option_text: To waste time
To work or study late into the night
To ruin something valuable
To light a room

questions.explanation: Idiom originating from the era of oil lamps — burning lamp oil late at night to keep working. Synonymous with 'pull an all-nighter'. Example — 'She burned the midnight oil to finish her research paper.'
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: To take a long route home
To make more effort than expected
To distance yourself from friends
To travel for work

questions.explanation: To do more than is strictly required, to give exceptional effort. Origin from the Biblical 'if any man shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain'. Example — 'Our team went the extra mile to deliver the project ahead of schedule.'
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: A fake reward
Something that seems bad at first but proves beneficial
A secret gift
A religious ritual

questions.explanation: An apparent setback that turns out to be an advantage. Example — 'Missing that flight was a blessing in disguise — the plane was delayed by 8 hours.' Synonym expressions — 'silver lining' (every cloud has a silver lining), 'a mixed blessing' (both good and bad elements).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'To cost an arm and a leg' means something is:

options.option_text: Very cheap
Very expensive
Physically dangerous
Difficult to obtain

questions.explanation: To be prohibitively expensive. Example — 'That designer dress cost an arm and a leg.' Related exam-favourites for 'expensive' — 'pay through the nose', 'a pretty penny'. Opposites ('cheap') — 'dirt cheap', 'for a song'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Avoid difficult decisions
Accept and face a difficult situation with courage
Reject a proposal outright
Hurry with a task

questions.explanation: To do something unpleasant but necessary with determination. Origin — in the era before anaesthetics, wounded soldiers literally had a bullet or strap placed between the teeth to bite on during battlefield surgery. Example — 'He had to bite the bullet and admit his mistake to the team.'
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'Hit the nail on the head' means:

options.option_text: To injure someone
To describe something exactly right
To finish a job perfectly
To be very lucky

questions.explanation: To state the truth or solve a problem with precision. Example — 'Her analysis of the failure hit the nail on the head — poor quality control.' Related — 'spot-on', 'bang on'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'To throw in the towel' means to:

options.option_text: Clean up
Give up or surrender
Start fresh
Attack the opponent

questions.explanation: To admit defeat and quit. Origin — in boxing, a trainer traditionally throws a towel into the ring to indicate that their fighter is unable to continue. Example — 'After months of failed negotiations, the company finally threw in the towel.' Synonyms — 'call it quits', 'give up the ghost'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: When the factory supervisor 'turned a blind eye' to repeated safety violations, he was essentially:

options.option_text: taking swift disciplinary action on the offenders
deliberately choosing to ignore known misconduct
reporting the violations to higher authorities
genuinely unaware of the misconduct taking place

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'turn a blind eye' means to be aware of wrongdoing yet deliberately choose not to act on it. Option D is the key distractor — the idiom specifically implies conscious awareness combined with wilful inaction, unlike genuine unawareness.

questions.stem: The idiom 'bite off more than you can chew' is best illustrated by which of the following scenarios?

options.option_text: A student who revises all chapters thoroughly before exams
A manager who takes on far more projects than he can handle
An athlete who trains rigorously for an upcoming championship
A chef who tries an unfamiliar but straightforward new recipe

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'bite off more than you can chew' describes taking on responsibilities that exceed one's capacity. Option C is a distractor — rigorous training is ambitious but feasible; the idiom requires that the task genuinely surpasses the person's ability or bandwidth.

questions.stem: A literature teacher who asks students to 'read between the lines' of a passage wants them to:

options.option_text: re-read the passage slowly and several times aloud
identify only the literal and explicitly stated facts
grasp the implied meaning not directly stated in text
focus on the grammatical structure of every sentence

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'reading between the lines' means inferring unstated or implied meanings beyond the surface text. Option B is the main distractor — it describes the opposite, purely literal reading, which is precisely what the idiom asks students to move beyond.

questions.stem: The surprise-party organiser 'let the cat out of the bag' by accident. The host was disappointed primarily because:

options.option_text: the catering arrangements turned out to be very costly
the carefully kept secret had been revealed prematurely
the invited guests declined to attend the function
the venue had cancelled the booking at the last minute

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'let the cat out of the bag' means to accidentally disclose a secret. Options C and D describe logistical failures unrelated to the idiom; the host's disappointment here stems purely from the premature revelation that destroyed the element of surprise.

questions.stem: A politician who visits his home constituency 'once in a blue moon' is indicating that such visits are:

options.option_text: scheduled on fixed dates and completely predictable
extremely rare events that happen only very occasionally
mandatory visits required by constitutional obligations
undertaken only during elections or major festive seasons

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'once in a blue moon' denotes something that happens very rarely. Option D is a tempting distractor since election-season visits are indeed infrequent, but the idiom conveys general extreme rarity rather than any seasonal or event-driven pattern.

questions.stem: A colleague who 'has a chip on his shoulder' about being passed over for promotion will most likely:

options.option_text: redouble his efforts to earn recognition through results
remain cheerful and indifferent to any career setbacks
harbour deep resentment over a perceived unfair slight
openly congratulate the promoted colleague with warmth

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'a chip on one's shoulder' describes a persistent grievance or resentment born from a perceived injustice. Option A is the most tempting distractor — while some react to setbacks with renewed effort, the idiom specifically captures lingering bitterness and a grudge, not motivated ambition.

questions.stem: In high-stakes strategy meetings, a leader who 'cuts the Gordian knot' earns admiration because he:

options.option_text: analyses every risk factor before taking any cautious step
gathers extensive team consensus through long consultations
resolves a complex deadlock through one bold decisive move
delegates all difficult decisions to specialist committees

questions.explanation: C is correct: the idiom derives from Alexander the Great, who sliced the legendary Gordian Knot — an intricate knot that no one could untie — rather than attempting to untie it. It means solving an intractable problem with a single bold, unconventional action. Option A (cautious analysis) is the direct opposite of the decisive boldness the idiom celebrates; Option B (lengthy consensus) embodies the very delay the idiom transcends.
